doc.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: Baltimore scenes, the Royal Theater and his brother's records
summary: Katz describes Baltimore's separate white and black scenes, seeing Ellington at the Royal Theater, and his brother's 78s.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Was Baltimore a good place to grow up in as far as music?
No. But it was for me.
You almost said yes, and then you said no. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
I thought you meant as a city. No but that’s like that guy says in there, you see that movie “The Tannenbaums?”
He said — Gene Hackman, the daughter — he’s got a bunch of dysfunctional kids, so one of the daughters says, “You don’t even know my middle name.” And he says, “That’s a trick question.”

Um what I mean was that Baltimore normally would not be a good place to grow up in music, it wasn’t any main scene. There were two scenes, there was a white jazz scene and a black jazz scene, which is not unusual, that’s the American Way at that time, and I gravitated, there was a very lively black scene down the strip called Pennsylvania Avenue which was sort of the 125th Street of Baltimore. And they had a theater which was the Baltimore counterpart of the Apollo. It was called the Royal Theater. And everybody played there, all the bands. And so I used to hang out there as a teenager. I was totally smitten. When I went to see Duke Ellington one time and the band rose out of the — you’ve heard this story before — well I mean for your generation I don’t know who it was but I don’t think it was the Beatles, whatever, to see this orchestra rise out of the floor on a riser, you know, behind the scrim, and they’re in white tails, and Sonny Greer is on like a throne behind the band with the chimes and whatever, and then to hear that sound and see Duke, I mean that was epiphany. Well that was one of the things. I saw Fats Waller down there. I saw everybody. And that had a big effect on me. And my brother fortunately was a pioneer record collector, when nobody where I grew up, very few knew or cared about jazz or collected. He and his buddy bought these 78s as they came out for 35 cents a piece, of all the greats, Louis Armstrong, so I used to hear all this stuff around the house all the time. And that started me really. And you will hear variations on this from a lot of musicians. Older brother or something, some event or something that drew them in.
You got it in your ear.

Got it in my ear and there was an interesting wrinkle to this though, he used to play me a lot of Benny Goodman records and he and his buddy would make me dance when I was a little kid and all this kind of — you know he was six years older than me, so he’s like—
Yup, he ruled the roost as far as you’re concerned.
He ruled my roost. I don’t know about your family but — you got an older brother?

Okay. So I didn’t pay much attention, I liked it all right, and then my mother would make me take piano lessons at the Peabody Conservatory which I was not a good student. I really cheated ‘cause I didn’t really want to learn to read so I used to watch this fat lady © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
